title: Annuities & loan repayments
examples: How do I calculate the total interest paid over the life of a loan?
What is the difference between compound interest and simple interest in this context?
Can you show me an example using a loan that is paid monthly instead of yearly?

explain.say: Today we learn about annuities and loan repayments. These help us find regular payments over time. We will look at present and future values first.

items: Learn about annuities and loan repayments
Look at present and future values

explain.say: Future value is what a series of payments grows to later. Think of it as the total lump sum you will have. We use the future value annuity formula for this.
Present value is what a series of payments is worth today. This is often used for loan repayments. We use the present value annuity formula here.
An amortisation table shows how payments cover principal and interest. Each payment reduces the loan balance and pays interest on the remaining amount. Let us look at a simple car loan example.

faq.q: What is the difference between an annuity and a single lump sum payment?
faq.a: An annuity involves a series of equal payments over time. A lump sum is just one payment made all at once.
asks: Is an annuity like making many small payments?

faq.q: Do I always use the same interest rate for the whole loan?
faq.a: Usually, the interest rate remains constant for the term of the loan. However, some loans might adjust rates periodically.
asks: Is the rate fixed for the whole loan?

faq.q: Why do we need amortisation tables for loans?
faq.a: These tables show the breakdown of every payment. They clearly separate how much goes to interest and how much reduces the actual loan amount.
asks: What does an amortisation table show?
How do I see where my money goes each month?

faq.q: If I pay extra on my loan, how does that affect the table?
faq.a: Paying extra directly reduces the principal balance faster. This means you pay less interest overall and pay off the loan sooner.
asks: Can I pay extra to lower my loan?
Will paying more help me save on interest?

faq.q: Is the formula for present value the same as future value?
faq.a: No, they are different. Future value projects growth forward in time. Present value discounts future money back to today's worth.
asks: Are PV and FV formulas interchangeable?
Which formula do I use if I know the end amount?

facts: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals.
The present value calculation discounts future cash flows back to today's value.
In an amortisation table, the interest paid is calculated on the outstanding loan balance.
The total payments made over the life of a loan must equal the original principal plus total interest.

quiz.say: A loan of one thousand dollars is repaid over five years with annual interest of six percent. What is the required annual payment?
quiz.why: This requires finding the payment (PMT) using the present value annuity formula, which correctly calculates the fixed payment amount.

wrong.0: This might be calculated using the future value formula instead of the present value formula.
wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the payment by simply dividing the total interest by the number of years.
wrong.3: This assumes simple interest repayment, ignoring the compounding effect of interest on the remaining balance.

quiz.say: If you invest five hundred dollars today at three percent interest for ten years, what is its future value?
quiz.why: This is a single lump sum calculation, requiring the standard compound interest formula for future value.

wrong.0: This incorrectly assumes zero interest is earned over the ten-year period.
wrong.1: This might be calculated by only adding ten percent of the original amount as interest.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the value using simple interest over the entire period.

quiz.say: A loan of twenty thousand dollars is paid off over four years with an annual interest rate of five percent. What is the required annual payment?
quiz.why: We must use the present value annuity formula to find the fixed payment that amortises the initial loan amount over the given term.

wrong.0: This might result from incorrectly applying a simple interest calculation to the principal.
wrong.1: This incorrectly adds the total interest amount to the principal amount.
wrong.3: This suggests dividing the principal by the number of years, ignoring all interest costs.
